security.summary: PolySchnack has a thoughtfully designed authorization core (central permissions.get_access_level with read/write/full levels, API-key rights caps, hashed API keys with expiry, an explicit SSRF validator for BYOK endpoints, a path-traversal guard in the recovery router, safe list-form subprocess calls and parameterised SQL everywhere), but that core is not applied consistently, and several ingress points bypass it entirely. The most serious issues are: an unauthenticated URL-import endpoint that hands an attacker-controlled string straight to yt-dlp (server-side request forgery into the internal Docker/ASR network plus yt-dlp argument injection, since the URL is not separated from the option list by '--'), a transcript download route with no access check at all, cross-tenant transcript disclosure via global content-hash duplicate detection on upload, an OpenAI-compatible transcription proxy whose 'API key required' dependency silently accepts anonymous sessions, and a shipped dummy SESSION_SECRET in compose.oidc.yml which — because Starlette session cookies carry the is_admin flag and Fernet credential encryption is derived from the same secret — turns into admin-session forgery and decryptable stored credentials. Checked and found CLEAN: no SQL injection (SQLModel/SQLAlchemy statements are parameterised; the only f-string SQL in db._auto_migrate builds identifiers from the model metadata, never from request data); no eval/exec/os.system/shell=True/pickle; every ffmpeg/ffprobe/crispasr/aligner invocation uses list argv with non-string-interpolated parameters (durations are floats, paths are server-generated UUID names); no dangerouslySetInnerHTML, innerHTML, document.write or eval anywhere in the React frontend; the service worker never caches /api/* or /health and ignores non-GET requests; no CORS middleware is registered (so no permissive cross-origin policy) and the session cookie keeps Starlette's httponly+SameSite=lax defaults with https_only derived from BASE_URL; no SSTI (render_template is only called with static templates); API-key tokens are 32-byte urlsafe randoms stored as SHA-256 hashes and looked up by hash, with expiry enforced; recovery/restore rejects path separators and '..'; benchmark sample ids are resolved against the manifest rather than joined into a path; robots.txt plus an X-Robots-Tag middleware cover share links; and no real secrets are committed (CI uses variables, .env is gitignored).

findings.title: Unauthenticated SSRF and yt-dlp argument injection in /api/recordings/from-url
findings.description: The endpoint requires no authentication (an anonymous cookie session is created on the fly) and performs no validation of the submitted URL — the project's own SSRF validator (app/llm_url.validate_llm_url, used for BYOK endpoints) is not applied here. Any internet user can make the webapp container fetch arbitrary URLs, reaching hosts only reachable from inside the compose network: http://docker-proxy:2375/containers/json, http://ps-pk-onnx:5092, http://crispr-align:5099, or cloud metadata at http://169.254.169.254/. Fetched bytes are stored as a recording the attacker owns and can download, and yt-dlp's stderr (which frequently echoes response details) is returned verbatim in the 400 detail, so this is not blind. Worse, the URL is appended as a bare positional argument with no '--' end-of-options separator, so a value beginning with '-' is parsed by yt-dlp as an option: --config-location=<path> (loads an attacker-plantable config file, which may itself contain --exec), --paths/-o (write files to arbitrary locations inside the container), --batch-file=/etc/passwd. Combined with the container running as root, this is a plausible path from an unauthenticated HTTP request to code/file-write inside the webapp container.
findings.evidence:
proc = subprocess.run(
    [
        "yt-dlp",
        "-f", "ba/b",
        "-x",
        "-o", out_template,
        "--no-playlist",
        url.strip(),
    ],
findings.recommendation: Require an authenticated (non-anonymous) identity for the import; run url.strip() through validate_llm_url (extended to reject non-http(s) schemes, private/loopback/link-local IPs and DNS names resolving to them, re-checked after redirects); reject any URL not starting with 'http://' or 'https://' and pass '--' immediately before the URL so it can never be parsed as an option; add '--no-config-locations' (or --ignore-config) and a rate limit per identity; return a generic error instead of raw yt-dlp stderr.

findings.title: GET /api/recordings/{rid}/download has no access-control check
findings.description: Every other recording route resolves the caller's identity and calls ensure_access(...). The transcript export route does not: it takes no Request, never computes a uid, and never calls ensure_access. Anyone who ever learns a recording uid — a revoked share recipient, someone who received an anon share link that the owner has since switched off, a proxy/browser-history/referrer leak, or a holder of a read-capped API key — can fetch the complete transcript as txt/srt/vtt forever. Disabling the anon share link (POST /anon-link with enabled=false) does not close this hole, so the documented revocation mechanism is ineffective for the export path. The webapp test suite covers access control for get/audio/segments but never for download, confirming this is an oversight rather than a deliberate public route.
findings.recommendation: Add `request: Request` and the same two lines used by get_audio: `uid = _current_user(request, session)` and `ensure_access(session, rec, uid, "read", cap=_key_cap(request, session))`, and add a regression test to webapp/tests/test_access_in_routes.py.

findings.title: Cross-user transcript disclosure via global content-hash duplicate detection on upload
findings.description: The upload endpoint looks up an existing Recording by content_hash across ALL users and, on a hit, returns the full serialised recording of that foreign row — including `text` (the complete transcript), `segments`, `uid`, `user_id` and the audio/download URLs. An attacker who possesses (or can guess/obtain) the same audio file another user uploaded — a circulated WhatsApp voice message, a published podcast episode, a leaked meeting recording — simply uploads it and receives the other user's transcription plus the uid, which then unlocks the unauthenticated download route (see the finding above). The url_import router already fixed exactly this bug ('Dedup NUR innerhalb derselben Identitaet', line 136-140) but the fix was never carried over to the main upload path.
findings.recommendation: Scope the duplicate query to the current identity: `.where(Recording.content_hash == content_hash, Recording.user_id == uid)` (resolve uid before the lookup), exactly as url_import.py does.

findings.title: OpenAI-compatible transcription proxy is effectively unauthenticated
findings.description: POST /v1/audio/transcriptions is guarded by _require_identity, documented as '401 ohne gueltigen Key' and advertised in the OpenAPI schema with an ApiKeyAuth security requirement. But current_identity only enforces a key when an Authorization: Bearer header is present; without one it falls through to ensure_anonymous_user() and returns a valid Identity. The endpoint therefore accepts any request with no credentials at all, exposing the entire GPU/ASR fleet as free compute to the internet. It also bypasses the paid-path gate: pricing.ensure_free_only is never called here, so an anonymous caller can select any backend in _ALLOWED_BACKENDS via the `backend` form field — including backends the anon gating in /api/recordings/{rid}/transcribe explicitly forbids — and the anon duration/size quotas from anon_limits are not applied either.
findings.recommendation: Reject requests without an Authorization header (raise 401 before calling current_identity, or add a `require_api_key` variant that returns 401 when identity.key_level is None), then run pricing.ensure_free_only and anon_limits.enforce_anon_limits on the resolved user before dispatching to a backend.

findings.title: Shipped dummy SESSION_SECRET allows forged admin sessions
findings.description: The OIDC overlay defaults SESSION_SECRET to the literal 'dummy-session-secret-change-me' when the variable is absent from .env, and OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET to 'dummy-client-secret-change-me'. Starlette's SessionMiddleware signs the session cookie with that key, and the session carries both `user_id` and `is_admin` (set in routers/auth.callback). Anyone who reads this public repository can mint a cookie for {"user_id": 1, "is_admin": true} against a deployment that forgot the .env entry and immediately reach /api/admin/* — which starts, stops and restarts containers and reads their logs through the docker-socket-proxy — plus /api/recovery/*, benchmark editing and every recording of user 1. The failure is silent: the stack starts normally and nothing warns the operator.
findings.evidence:
SESSION_SECRET: "${SESSION_SECRET:-dummy-session-secret-change-me}"
BASE_URL: "${BASE_URL:-https://polyschnack.example.com}"
findings.recommendation: Drop the defaults and use the required-variable form (`${SESSION_SECRET:?set SESSION_SECRET in .env}`) so compose refuses to start without it, and add a startup assertion in the webapp that raises when OIDC_ENABLED is true and SESSION_SECRET is empty or matches a known placeholder.

findings.title: Credential encryption key falls back to the literal string "dev"
findings.description: The Fernet key protecting BYOK LLM API keys (UserLlmEndpoint.api_key) and WebDAV delivery passwords (DeliveryTarget.config) is sha256(SESSION_SECRET or 'dev'). SESSION_SECRET has no default in config.py, and the base compose.yml leaves it commented out — main.py papers over that with a random per-process session key, so a deployment can run happily without ever setting it while every encrypted credential in app.db is protected by the publicly known constant sha256(b'dev'). Anyone with a copy of the SQLite file (backup, volume snapshot, the ./DATA bind mount, an admin VACUUM artefact) recovers the plaintext third-party API keys and WebDAV passwords with three lines of code. The key is also computed once at import time, so rotating SESSION_SECRET silently makes all stored credentials undecryptable rather than re-wrapping them.
findings.recommendation: Introduce a dedicated POLYSCHNACK_CRYPTO_KEY (or require SESSION_SECRET) and fail fast at import when it is unset instead of falling back to 'dev'; consider storing a key id alongside each ciphertext so rotation is possible.

findings.title: Upload reads the entire request body into memory before the size check
findings.description: `raw = await file.read()` materialises the whole multipart part in RAM and only then compares its length against MAX_UPLOAD_SIZE_MB (default 1024 MB) — the 413 fires after the memory has already been consumed, so the limit does not limit anything. The ps-webapp container is capped at 4 GB; a handful of concurrent multi-gigabyte POSTs (no authentication, no rate limit) OOM-kills it, and the same body is then copied again by prepare_storage/ffmpeg. Two related problems in the same handler: the file is written to disk (line 541) BEFORE enforce_anon_limits runs (line 555), so a rejected over-quota upload still leaves a full-size orphan file in AUDIO_DIR, and the identical read-everything pattern exists in openai_proxy.create_transcription (line 126) and transcribe_range (Path(...).read_bytes(), line 1215).
findings.evidence:
max_bytes = settings.MAX_UPLOAD_SIZE_MB * 1024 * 1024
raw = await file.read()
if len(raw) > max_bytes:
    raise HTTPException(status_code=413, detail=f"file too large (max {settings.MAX_UPLOAD_SIZE_MB} MB)")
findings.recommendation: Stream the upload to a temp file in bounded chunks and abort with 413 as soon as the running total exceeds the limit (also check the Content-Length header up front), enforce the anon quota before writing to AUDIO_DIR, and reject oversized bodies at the reverse proxy (client_max_body_size) as a second layer.

findings.title: Recovery of orphaned audio is unauthenticated when OIDC is disabled
findings.description: _require_admin returns immediately when OIDC is off — which is the default configuration of compose.yml (the OIDC block is commented out). In that deployment any anonymous visitor can call GET /api/recovery/scan to enumerate every orphaned audio file in AUDIO_DIR (names, sizes, ages) and POST /api/recovery/restore to materialise any of them as a Recording with user_id=None. Because permissions.get_access_level grants 'read' to everyone for rows with user_id None, the restored audio and its transcript become readable by every visitor — turning other users' abandoned uploads (which the module docstring itself calls 'potenziell sensible Audiodaten') into public content. Restore is also an unbounded disk-doubling primitive (it copies the file) with no rate limit.
findings.recommendation: Mirror deps.require_admin: when OIDC is disabled, deny the route (403) instead of allowing it, or gate the whole router behind an explicit POLYSCHNACK_ENABLE_RECOVERY env flag intended for local development only; assign restored recordings to a real owner rather than user_id=None.

findings.title: Unauthenticated pip install trigger at POST /api/models/vad/download
findings.description: The whole /api/models router has no dependencies and no admin gate. POST /api/models/vad/download spawns a background thread that runs `pip install silero-vad` with the interpreter's own privileges (the container runs as root) and then downloads a model from the network. Any unauthenticated caller can trigger installation of a third-party package into the running production container and repeatedly cause network fetches and CPU/disk churn; if PyPI or the package is compromised, an outsider — not an operator — chose the moment of installation. The sibling endpoints also expose an unauthenticated internal-topology map (/api/models/status and /services return the ASR/diar/aligner service URLs, device information and raw exception strings).
findings.evidence:
@router.post("/vad/download")
def download_vad() -> DownloadResponse:
    ...
    thread = threading.Thread(target=_download_vad, daemon=True)
    thread.start()
...
        subprocess.run(
            [sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "silero-vad"],
findings.recommendation: Put the download endpoints behind Depends(require_admin), and preferably remove runtime pip installation entirely — bake silero-vad into the image (the Dockerfile already installs the other dependencies) so the running container never needs a package manager.

findings.title: WebDAV delivery target performs unvalidated authenticated SSRF
findings.description: DeliveryTarget config accepts an arbitrary `url` that is later PUT to with the stored credentials and the transcript body; unlike the BYOK LLM endpoints (routers/llm_endpoints.py calls validate_llm_url) the targets router applies no URL validation at all. A user can therefore point a target at http://docker-proxy:2375/..., http://ps-pk-onnx:5092/... or 169.254.169.254 and have the server issue authenticated requests into the internal network, exfiltrating transcripts to an arbitrary host at the same time. Note that the targets router's require_authenticated gate is a no-op when OIDC is disabled (deps.py line 36), so in the default compose deployment any anonymous visitor can create such a target. The destination path is also built by concatenating rec.original_name (user-controlled, may contain '../') into the URL.
findings.evidence:
dest = f"{url}/{path}/{rec.original_name}.txt" if path else f"{url}/{rec.original_name}.txt"
r = httpx.put(
    dest,
    auth=(cfg["username"], decrypt(cfg["password"])),
    content=(rec.text or "").encode("utf-8"),
    timeout=60,
)
findings.recommendation: Run cfg['url'] through validate_llm_url when the target is created/updated and again immediately before delivery (DNS may have changed), disable redirects on the httpx call, and percent-encode / sanitise rec.original_name before putting it in the path.

findings.title: All containers run as root and the webapp can drive the Docker daemon
findings.description: None of the images drop privileges: the webapp Dockerfile has no USER directive, and approach-a/Dockerfile creates a 'polyschnack' user and then explicitly documents 'Run as root so the model download volume works without permission issues' (line 48). The webapp additionally holds network access to docker-proxy with CONTAINERS=1 and POST=1, i.e. it can start/stop/restart containers and read their logs. Any code-execution or file-write bug in the webapp (see the yt-dlp argument-injection finding) therefore executes as root, can rewrite the bind-mounted ./DATA volume and the SQLite database, and can manipulate containers on the host. The optional backends also publish unauthenticated inference APIs directly on host ports 5092-5097 (compose.yml line 38, compose.backends.yml), so anyone who can reach the host bypasses the webapp's quota and paid-path gating entirely.
findings.evidence:
ENV DATA_DIR=/data \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

EXPOSE 8088

CMD ["uv", "run", "uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8088"]
findings.recommendation: Add a non-root USER to each image (chown the mounted volumes in the entrypoint or via an init container), set read_only/ no-new-privileges / cap_drop: [ALL] in compose, bind the backend ports to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0, and set DOCKER_PROXY_TOKEN so the proxy is not reachable by anything else on the compose network.

findings.title: No rate limiting: unauthenticated endpoints create users, jobs and long-running subprocesses
findings.description: There is no rate limiting anywhere in the application. Every request without a session cookie inserts a new User row (unbounded DB growth from a trivial loop), each anonymous user then gets a fresh 500 MB disk quota and 100 MB upload allowance, and the URL import can occupy a yt-dlp subprocess for up to 600 s per call with a built-in automatic retry — all without authentication. The global queue cap (POLYSCHNACK_MAX_QUEUE_LEN=20) is shared across all users, so a single anonymous client can fill it and deny transcription to everyone else; peaks/preview generation spawns additional unbounded ffmpeg threads (_schedule_peaks) per upload. The retention sweep only reclaims anon users after POLYSCHNACK_ANON_RETENTION_MINUTES of inactivity, which does not help against an active attacker.
findings.evidence:
if not user or user.kind != "anonymous":
        user = User(sub=f"anon:{uuid.uuid4().hex}", kind="anonymous",
                    display_name=generate_name())
        session.add(user)
        session.commit()
findings.recommendation: Add per-IP and per-identity rate limits (slowapi/limits or reverse-proxy level) on /api/recordings, /api/recordings/from-url, /v1/audio/transcriptions and /api/models/*; cap concurrent yt-dlp/ffmpeg subprocesses with a semaphore; make the queue limit per-user rather than global; and only materialise an anonymous User row when the request actually creates data.

findings.title: OIDC callback never validates the ID token and the nonce store grows unbounded
findings.description: The callback validates `state` (good) but the generated `nonce` is only popped from a module-level dict — it is never compared against the nonce claim of an id_token, and the id_token is never fetched, decoded or signature-verified at all; identity comes solely from the userinfo endpoint. That is acceptable only because the access token is obtained over a direct back-channel TLS call, so it is a hardening gap rather than an exploitable bypass today, but it silently breaks if the flow ever changes to accept tokens from the front channel. Two operational issues in the same file: _nonce_store is a process-global dict whose entries are only removed on a successful callback, so repeatedly hitting /auth/login grows memory without bound (and the store makes the app single-worker-only), and _discover/_exchange_code/userinfo call httpx without any timeout, so a hanging IdP ties up worker threads indefinitely.
findings.recommendation: Verify the id_token (signature via the issuer JWKS, iss/aud/exp and the nonce claim) or drop the nonce entirely to avoid implying a check that does not happen; store state/nonce in the signed session cookie instead of a global dict; add explicit timeouts to all three httpx calls.

findings.title: Swagger UI loads scripts from a third-party CDN without integrity pinning
findings.description: /api-docs (unauthenticated) and the aligner's /docs embed swagger-ui-bundle.js from unpkg.com with a floating major-version tag and no Subresource Integrity hash or CSP. A compromise or hijack of that CDN path executes attacker JavaScript in the application's origin, where it can read the session cookie's effects (same-origin API calls run with the user's cookies) and, since persistAuthorization is enabled, exfiltrate API keys that users paste into the Authorize box.
findings.evidence: <script src="https://unpkg.com/swagger-ui-dist@5/swagger-ui-bundle.js"></script>
findings.recommendation: Vendor swagger-ui-dist into app/static and serve it locally (or pin an exact version with an integrity= hash and crossorigin=anonymous), and add a Content-Security-Policy response header restricting script-src to 'self'.

findings.title: Internal error text is reflected to unauthenticated clients
findings.description: Several handlers put raw subprocess or exception output into the HTTP response: yt-dlp stderr (500 chars), ffmpeg concat stderr in merge_recordings (recordings.py:713), docker-proxy error strings including internal URLs and HTTP bodies (docker_proxy.py:86, surfaced as 503 details in admin/transcribe), OIDC exception text (auth.py:105/134/145) and the container log tails in the admin start-timeout response. This hands an attacker internal hostnames, filesystem paths, tool versions and configuration details for free, and combines with the SSRF finding to make internal responses observable.
findings.evidence:
err = (proc.stderr or "no output")[:500]
log.warning("yt-dlp failed for url=%s: %s", url[:80], err)
hint = _ytdlp_error_hint(err, url)
detail = f"yt-dlp failed: {err}"
findings.recommendation: Log the raw text server-side and return a short generic message plus a correlation id to the client; reserve detailed diagnostics for admin-gated endpoints.

findings.title: Anonymous share access is a boolean flag, so revocation is per-flag and uid secrecy is the only control
findings.description: Recording.share_token is a bool, not a secret: get_access_level grants 'read' to every non-owner as soon as the flag is true, and the only thing protecting the recording is the 32-hex uid in the /r/<uid> URL. The uid is a uuid4 hex so it is not guessable, but it is a bearer capability that appears in browser history, referrer headers, reverse-proxy access logs and every API path — and it is permanent (there is no per-link token to rotate, so re-enabling a link resurrects access for everyone who ever saw the URL). Combined with the missing check on the download route, disabling a link does not fully revoke access today.
findings.recommendation: Store an actual random share token separate from the uid, require it as a query/header value on share access, and regenerate it whenever the link is toggled off and on so old URLs die.

findings.title: Held-out benchmark audio is downloadable by id
findings.description: The public /samples listing correctly filters out held_out samples, but /audio/{id} and /preview/{id} resolve the id against ALL manifest entries (benchmark_service.sample_audio_path iterates m['samples'] without a held_out filter), so anyone who learns or predicts a held-out sample id (ids follow the deterministic pattern <category>_<nnn>) can download the anti-gaming reserve audio. No path traversal is possible — the id must match a manifest entry — so the impact is limited to benchmark integrity.
findings.recommendation: Filter on `s['status'] == 'active' and not s['held_out']` inside sample_audio_path (or in the routes), returning 404 for held-out ids.

smells.summary: The webapp mixes async FastAPI handlers with fully synchronous, minutes-long work (yt-dlp, ffmpeg, blocking ASR HTTP calls with a 3600 s timeout), so a single URL import or proxy transcription freezes the entire server event loop — this is the most damaging class of defect found. A second cluster is unscoped/absent authorization: the upload duplicate check matches content hashes across all users and returns the other user's transcript, and GET /recordings/{uid}/download performs no access check at all. The threading in queue.py is sound in its locking but has two behavioural defects: workers block on a per-backend semaphore after dequeuing (head-of-line starvation across backends) and cancel() races the worker's status transition. Resource handling leaks in several places: rejected anonymous uploads leave orphan files on disk, permanently-failing preview generation makes the backfill loop re-run a 600 s ffmpeg transcode every 30 s forever, and SMTP delivery has no timeout so a worker slot can hang indefinitely. Test coverage is broad (nearly every module is exercised), so the gaps below are behavioural, not untested-code gaps.

findings.title: Blocking ASR call inside async handler freezes the whole server for up to an hour
findings.description: create_transcription is `async def`, but `client.transcribe(...)` is a synchronous httpx call — every adapter uses `with httpx.Client(timeout=3600)` (asr_client/adapters/*.py). A single POST /v1/audio/transcriptions of a 30-minute file occupies the asyncio event loop thread for the entire transcription: /health, the SPA, all polling and every other API request stall until the backend answers or the 3600 s timeout expires. The upload path avoids this only by accident (transcribe_ep is a sync `def`, so Starlette runs it in the threadpool).
findings.evidence:
async def create_transcription(...):
    ...
    client = get_client(target)
    result = client.transcribe(raw, filename, mime)   # sync httpx, timeout=3600
findings.recommendation: Make the handler a plain `def` (Starlette threadpool) or wrap the blocking part in `await run_in_threadpool(...)`. Same rule for every handler that touches ffmpeg/httpx-sync.

findings.title: yt-dlp + ffmpeg run synchronously inside an async handler (up to ~20 min event-loop stall)
findings.description: import_from_url is `async def` and calls subprocess.run(yt-dlp, timeout=600) — twice on failure (retry at line 86) — then src_path.read_bytes(), prepare_storage() (ffmpeg, timeout=600) and stored.write_bytes(), all on the event loop thread. Import a slow/blocked YouTube URL and the server answers nothing at all for up to 20 minutes; the frontend's 2 s polling piles up requests and the health check fails, which in Docker can trigger a container restart mid-import.
findings.evidence:
async def import_from_url(...):
    proc = subprocess.run(["yt-dlp", ...], timeout=600)
    ...
    retry_proc = subprocess.run(["yt-dlp", ...], timeout=600)
findings.recommendation: Change to `def` (threadpool) or offload the download/conversion to the existing background-thread mechanism and return 202 with a recording row in state 'importing'.

findings.title: Whole upload buffered in RAM inside an async handler; size limit checked after the read
findings.description: upload_recording is `async def` and does `raw = await file.read()` before checking MAX_UPLOAD_SIZE_MB (default 1024 MB, config.py:62). A 1 GB upload therefore lives in RAM as `raw`, plus a second full copy as ffmpeg's output in prepare_storage (audio_utils.convert_to_mp3 uses capture_output=True), plus the blake2b pass — ~2-3 GB peak in a container the codebase itself documents as 2 GB (peaks.py header). A client sending 5 GB is buffered in full and only then gets its 413. The subsequent ffmpeg conversion (600 s timeout) and stored.write_bytes() also block the event loop, as in the two findings above.
findings.recommendation: Stream the UploadFile to a temp path in chunks, aborting as soon as the byte count exceeds the limit (also honour Content-Length early), hash while streaming, and run the ffmpeg step off the loop with file paths instead of pipes.

findings.title: Upload duplicate check is global — returns another user's recording and transcript
findings.description: The content_hash lookup has no user_id filter, and the response embeds the full `_recording_to_dict(existing)` — including `text`, `segments`, `original_name`, `uid` and `user_id`. Scenario: Alice uploads meeting.mp3 and transcribes it; Bob (who has the same file, e.g. a shared podcast/WhatsApp voice note) uploads it and receives Alice's transcript, her recording uid and her user_id in the 201 response — without any share. url_import.py:135 got this right (`existing.user_id == current_user_id`); the upload path did not.
findings.recommendation: Scope the query with `Recording.user_id == uid` (compute uid before the lookup), as the URL-import path already does.

findings.title: GET /recordings/{uid}/download has no access check
findings.description: Every sibling endpoint calls ensure_access(...) (audio, preview, get, transcribe, delete); download_transcript does not even resolve a user. Anyone holding the uid gets txt/srt/vtt of the full transcript, regardless of ownership, of share level, and — the concrete failure — after the owner has switched the anon share link OFF via POST /recordings/{rid}/anon-link {enabled:false}: the recipient's saved /download URL keeps returning the transcript forever. The route also has no `request` parameter at all, so API-key caps (key_level) can never apply to it.
findings.recommendation: Add `request: Request` and `ensure_access(session, rec, _current_user(request, session), "read", cap=_key_cap(request, session))`, and add a regression case to tests/test_access_in_routes.py.

findings.title: Queue worker blocks on the per-backend semaphore after dequeuing → cross-backend starvation
findings.description: A worker pops the next job from the global priority queue and only then calls sem.acquire() for that job's backend, holding the worker thread hostage. Worker count = sum of all endpoint capacities. Scenario: backends A and B, concurrency 1 each → 2 workers. Enqueue A1, A2, then B1. Worker1 takes A1 and runs it; worker2 takes A2 and blocks on A's semaphore; B1 stays in the FIFO with no free worker, so an idle backend B does nothing until A1 finishes — the ETA/position shown to the B user is pure fiction. With three queued A jobs and 2 workers, B is starved for two full transcriptions.
findings.evidence:
_, _, rec_id = self._fifo.get(timeout=1.0)
...
sem = self._semaphore_for(job.backend)
sem.acquire()
findings.recommendation: Use one queue (or one worker pool) per backend, or `sem.acquire(blocking=False)` and re-queue the job when the endpoint is saturated so the worker can pick up work for another backend.

findings.title: cancel() races the worker: a cancelled job is still transcribed
findings.description: The worker reads the Job under the lock, then releases it and sets job.status = "processing" only after sem.acquire() returns. cancel() checks `job.status != 'queued'` under the lock. Timing: worker dequeues rec 42 and blocks on a busy semaphore; the user presses ✕; cancel() sees status still 'queued', deletes the job dict entry and resets the DB row to status='uploaded'; the semaphore frees, and the worker — holding its own `job` reference — proceeds to set_processing() and process_recording(42). The user sees a cancelled job start by itself, and if they meanwhile press transcribe again, enqueue succeeds (the dict entry is gone) so the same recording is transcribed twice concurrently, both writing update_result for the same row.
findings.evidence:
with self._lock:
    job = self._jobs.get(rec_id)
...
sem.acquire()
try:
    job.status = "processing"
findings.recommendation: Claim the job atomically: inside one `with self._lock` block re-fetch it, verify it is still queued, and flip it to 'processing' before doing any blocking work; treat a missing entry as cancelled and skip.

findings.title: Anonymous quota is enforced after the file is written — orphan files, quota bypass
findings.description: stored.write_bytes(audio_data) happens at line 541; enforce_anon_limits() raises 409/413 at line 555. On rejection no Recording row is created, so the file in AUDIO_DIR is referenced by nothing: retention.sweep and delete_recording only unlink paths reachable from rows, so it is never cleaned up. An anonymous user who repeatedly uploads 101 MB files past the 100 MB limit fills the data volume with invisible files while still being told 'limit reached'. The quota itself is also check-then-act: two concurrent uploads both read the same SUM(size_bytes) and both pass.
findings.evidence:
stored.write_bytes(audio_data)
...
enforce_anon_limits(session, ..., len(audio_data), est_duration_s)
findings.recommendation: Validate size/duration/quota before persisting (write to a temp file, probe, check, then move into AUDIO_DIR), and unlink the temp file in an except/finally around the limit check.

findings.title: Peaks/preview backfill loops forever on files whose preview cannot be produced, and blocks all newer rows
findings.description: list_recordings_missing_peaks selects rows where preview_path IS NULL, ordered by id ASC, limit 2 — and _backfill_peaks_batch only persists something when a preview or peaks were produced. If compute_preview_path fails permanently (corrupt file, video container libmp3lame refuses, file missing), preview_path stays NULL and the very same two rows are selected again by the 30 s loop in main.py:139 — each pass spawning an ffmpeg transcode with a 600 s timeout. Result: permanent CPU burn and, because of the id-ASC + limit-2 ordering, no newer recording ever gets its peaks or preview. The 'no endless retry' guard described in the docstring only exists for waveform_peaks ([] marker), not for preview_path.
findings.evidence:
.where(or_(cast(Recording.waveform_peaks, String) == "null",
           Recording.waveform_peaks.is_(None),
           Recording.preview_path.is_(None)))
.order_by(Recording.id.asc()).limit(limit)
findings.recommendation: Persist a failure marker for the preview too (e.g. preview_path = '' or an attempt counter/timestamp column) and exclude marked rows from the query, mirroring the [] convention used for peaks.

findings.title: _auto_migrate uses the Session after its context manager closed it; ALTER TABLEs are never committed
findings.description: The `with Session(engine) as session:` block ends at line 121 (after the ALTER TABLE loop), but lines 124-153 keep using `session` for the stale-processing UPDATE, the backend-rename UPDATEs and the final commit. The ALTER TABLEs themselves are never committed inside their block — they survive only because pysqlite runs DDL in autocommit; any change to the driver/isolation_level (e.g. `create_engine(..., isolation_level=...)`, a switch to sqlite3 with autocommit disabled, or a future Postgres move) silently rolls the schema migration back while init_db reports success. The follow-up UPDATEs likewise depend on SQLAlchemy silently re-opening a closed Session.
findings.evidence:
session.exec(sa_text(sql))

    fix = sa_text("UPDATE recording SET status='uploaded' ...")
    session.exec(fix)      # <-- outside the with-block
    ...
    session.commit()
findings.recommendation: Put the whole migration inside one `with Session(engine) as session:` block and commit explicitly after the DDL loop; a test that asserts a migrated column survives a fresh engine/connection would have caught this.

findings.title: _peaks_inflight guard is check-then-act and shared by two independent schedulers
findings.description: _schedule_peaks does `if rec_id in _peaks_inflight: return` then `.add(...)` without a lock, and _backfill_peaks_batch (running in the peaks-backfill thread) adds/discards the same ids. Two failure modes: (a) GET /recordings and the transcribe endpoint can both pass the membership test for the same id and start two ffmpeg full decodes of the same 300 MB file — precisely the CPU/RAM collapse the comment says was fixed; (b) when the backfill thread and a _schedule_peaks thread work on the same id, whichever finishes first calls discard(), clearing the flag while the other decode is still running, so a third decode can start. Both threads then write the same row from different sessions (last writer wins).
findings.recommendation: Guard the set with a threading.Lock (or use a dict of futures), and have the backfill skip ids that are already inflight instead of discarding them unconditionally.

findings.title: Public retention silently deletes admin-restored recordings an hour after recovery
findings.description: _purge_expired (run from init_db on every startup) deletes every Recording with user_id IS NULL older than PUBLIC_RETENTION_MINUTES (default 60) together with its file. recovery.recovery_restore deliberately creates restored orphans with user_id=None ('anonym — gehört niemandem, aber ist sichtbar'). An admin who recovers files after an incident loses them again — row and audio file — at the next restart occurring more than 60 minutes later, with no warning and no undo. The purge also has no guard against rows currently queued/processing.
findings.evidence:
expired = session.exec(select(_Recording).where(_Recording.user_id.is_(None), _Recording.created_at < datetime.utcnow() - timedelta(minutes=ret))).all()
for rec in expired: path.unlink(); session.delete(rec)
findings.recommendation: Mark restored rows (e.g. source='restored') and exclude them from the purge, and skip rows whose status is queued/processing.

findings.title: SMTP delivery has no timeout — a queue worker (and its endpoint slot) can hang forever
findings.description: smtplib.SMTP(host, port) is created without `timeout=`, so it inherits the global socket default (usually None = infinite). deliver() is called from process_recording inside the queue worker. A blackholed SMTP host (firewall DROP) parks the worker thread indefinitely; because the worker never releases the backend semaphore, that endpoint's capacity is permanently reduced and, with concurrency 1, the backend stops accepting jobs entirely. The stale-processing sweep will meanwhile mark the recording 'failed' even though the transcription actually succeeded.
findings.evidence: with smtplib.SMTP(settings.POLYSCHNACK_SMTP_HOST, settings.POLYSCHNACK_SMTP_PORT or 587) as s:
findings.recommendation: Pass an explicit timeout (e.g. 30 s) to smtplib.SMTP and wrap delivery in its own try/except so a delivery failure cannot outlive the job.

findings.title: vad._decode_to_wav runs ffmpeg without a timeout
findings.description: subprocess.run(ffmpeg, input=audio_bytes, capture_output=True) has no timeout, unlike every other ffmpeg call in the codebase (audio_utils 300/600 s, peaks 900 s, service 120 s). A malformed container that makes ffmpeg spin (or a stalled pipe) hangs the queue worker forever with the recording stuck at progress 12 'vad'. The function also decodes the whole file into a float32 numpy array (4 bytes/sample → ~1.4 GB for a 6 h recording) and trim_silence_with_offset decodes it a second time.
findings.evidence: p = subprocess.run(cmd, input=audio_bytes, capture_output=True, check=False)
findings.recommendation: Add a timeout and reuse the streaming/path-based decode approach from peaks.compute_peaks_path instead of materialising the whole waveform twice.

findings.title: transcribe-range: deterministic crop filename collides across recordings; no range validation
findings.description: crop_path is derived from the source stem plus int(start)-int(end), so calling the endpoint twice with the same (or rounding-equal, e.g. 10.2 and 10.7) range creates a second Recording row pointing at the same file path, silently overwriting the first crop's audio. Deleting either row unlinks the shared file, leaving the other row with status done and a 410 on /audio. start_sec/end_sec are also unvalidated: end < start yields a negative `-t` for ffmpeg (trim_audio, service.py:1046, which additionally has no subprocess timeout), and the whole source file is read into RAM via read_bytes() before trimming.
findings.evidence:
crop_path = parent / f"{stem}_crop_{int(start_sec)}-{int(end_sec)}.wav"
crop_path.write_bytes(trimmed)
findings.recommendation: Use a uuid4 filename like every other write path, validate 0 <= start < end <= duration, and let ffmpeg read the source by path instead of buffering it.

findings.title: Frontend stops polling for 'queued' recordings — the card freezes until a manual reload
findings.description: useRecordings only sets a refetchInterval when some recording has status === 'processing'; useStats only when stats.processing > 0. A recording that is enqueued behind another job gets status 'queued' (crud.set_queued), which matches neither predicate, so React Query stops polling entirely. If nothing else is processing in the user's own list — the normal case for a second user whose job waits behind a foreign job — the card shows 'queued' forever, including after the transcription has long finished. QueueWatcher polls separately but only renders the anonymised job list, not the card.
findings.evidence: return data.some((r) => r.status === "processing") ? 2000 : false;
findings.recommendation: Poll while status is 'queued' or 'processing' (and mirror that in useStats).

findings.title: Destructive endpoints ignore in-flight queue jobs
findings.description: merge_recordings deletes the source rows and unlinks their audio files, delete_recording_endpoint does the same for a single row, and retention.sweep deletes an anon user's recordings — none of them consult queue_manager.active_jobs_for / the job map. If the recording is currently being transcribed, the worker's audio_path.read_bytes() raises mid-job (or, worse, after the ASR stage the update_result silently writes to a deleted id and returns None), leaving the queue slot occupied and the user with no feedback. Merging while a source is queued additionally leaves a phantom queue entry whose rec_id no longer exists.
findings.evidence:
for rec in recs:
    path = Path(rec.stored_path)
    delete_recording(session, rec.id)
    path.unlink(missing_ok=True)
findings.recommendation: Reject (409) or cancel the job when a recording is queued/processing, using the same guard as the admin endpoint-stop path (queue_manager.active_jobs_for).

findings.title: Random per-process SESSION_SECRET orphans every anonymous user's recordings on restart
findings.description: When SESSION_SECRET is unset the app generates a fresh key at import time. Every anonymous identity lives in that signed cookie (anon_session.ensure_anonymous_user), and anonymous recordings are owned by the corresponding User row. After a restart (or with more than one uvicorn worker process, where each has its own key) the cookie no longer verifies, a brand-new anon user is created, and the previous recordings become invisible to their uploader — they remain on disk and in the DB until the retention sweep removes them. With multiple workers the identity flips per request, so uploads and transcribes land under different users and produce spurious 403s.
findings.evidence: secret_key=settings.SESSION_SECRET or secrets.token_urlsafe(32),
findings.recommendation: Fail fast (or persist a generated key to the data volume) when SESSION_SECRET is empty, and log a clear error rather than silently rotating identities.

findings.title: Estimated diarization split drops the tail of the transcript
findings.description: In the 'Status B' branch (no timestamps at all) each diarization segment takes n = round(len(words) * dur / total_dur) words. Because every n is rounded down as often as up and total_dur comes from the ASR duration rather than the sum of segment durations (silences between speakers are not covered), sum(n) is typically smaller than len(words_all): the remaining words are never emitted. Concretely, two speaker segments of 4 s each inside a 10 s recording over 100 words yield 40 + 40 = 80 words — 20 words of the transcript vanish from the segment list (rec.text still has them, so the UI shows a transcript longer than the sum of its segments). The timestamped path has an explicit leftover fix-up (lines 264-275); this branch has none.
findings.evidence:
n = int(round(len(words_all) * dur / total_dur))
chunk = words_all[w_idx:w_idx + n]
w_idx += n
findings.recommendation: Append the remaining words_all[w_idx:] to the last emitted segment, exactly as the timestamped path does.

findings.title: WaveformPlayer effect only depends on audioUrl — late-arriving peaks are ignored
findings.description: The setup effect reads peaks, durationHint and height but lists only [audioUrl]. Peaks are computed asynchronously after upload (_schedule_peaks) and arrive via the recordings poll, so on the first render peaks is null: WaveSurfer takes the browser full-decode path with a 60 s corruption timer, and when the peaks prop later flips to a 2000-value array nothing re-runs — the user keeps the slow path (or the 'Waveform data corrupted' banner) until a full remount. `height` changes are likewise ignored.
findings.recommendation: Add a cheap peaks identity (e.g. peaks?.length or a hasPeaks boolean) plus durationHint and height to the dependency array, or call ws.setOptions/reload when peaks first become available.

findings.title: process_recording reads ORM attributes from a detached instance
findings.description: `rec` is loaded in the `with Session(engine)` block that ends at line 697; scalar fields are copied into locals there, but rec.diarize_num_speakers / rec.diarize_min_duration_off / rec.diarize_method are read ~130 lines later, when the session is closed and the instance detached. It works today only because that block never commits (no attribute expiry). Adding any commit or an expire_on_commit session to that block turns the diarization call into a DetachedInstanceError, which the broad except turns into a failed recording with an opaque message.
findings.evidence: diar = _run_diarization(diar_path, num_speakers=rec.diarize_num_speakers, ...)
findings.recommendation: Copy the three diarize_* fields into locals alongside the other fields at the top.

findings.title: apply_aligned_words index drift when words precede the first segment
findings.description: The per-segment loop advances `wi` by len(seg_words), but words rejected by `ws >= s0 - 1e-3` are neither appended nor counted, so wi lags behind the actual scan position by the number of skipped words. For strictly ordered, non-overlapping segments the effect is only redundant rescanning (O(n*m)); if two segments overlap in time — possible with raw ASR segments that were not replaced by diarization — the same aligned word can be emitted into both segments, duplicating it in the karaoke display and in SRT/VTT output.
findings.recommendation: Track the real scan index (enumerate over by_time[wi:] and set wi to the last examined index + 1).

findings.title: peaks decode: odd-sized final chunk and stdout fd leak
findings.description: np.frombuffer(raw, dtype='<i2') raises ValueError ('buffer size must be a multiple of element size') if ffmpeg is killed mid-sample and the last read returns an odd byte count; the outer except swallows it and returns [], so the row keeps no peaks and (because of the backfill query above) is retried forever. Additionally, on the deadline path _chunks() returns while ffmpeg still holds a full stdout pipe, so proc.wait(timeout=30) raises TimeoutExpired and the already-computed peaks are discarded; proc.stdout is never closed explicitly in either function.
findings.evidence: arr = np.frombuffer(raw, dtype="<i2").astype(np.float32)
findings.recommendation: Trim the buffer to an even length (carry the odd byte to the next chunk), kill the process before waiting on the timeout path, and close proc.stdout in the finally block.

supplychain.summary: PolySchnack's supply chain is held together by mutable references: every ASR model weight (~5 GB of GGUF) is pulled from HuggingFace `resolve/main` with no checksum or signature, the CrispASR binaries come from GitHub release tarballs verified by nothing, and two images compile qwen3-asr.cpp from an unpinned `git clone --recursive` of upstream HEAD. Lockfiles exist (webapp/uv.lock, approach-a/uv.lock, package-lock.json with full integrity hashes) but the Docker builds bypass all of them — the webapp image copies only pyproject.toml before `uv sync`, runs `npm install` rather than `npm ci`, and adds a floating `yt-dlp>=2026.05.29`; approach-a installs a wholly unpinned requirements.txt as root with `--break-system-packages`. Base images are tag-pinned without digests, several are `:latest` (tecnativa/docker-socket-proxy, alpine, all compose services), and node:20-slim reached EOL on 2026-04-30. The sharpest single item is `polyschnack-manage.sh selfupdate`, which overwrites the script and backends.yaml from the network with only a `bash -n` syntax check, after which URLs from that same YAML are string-interpolated into a `docker run alpine sh -c` command line.

findings.title: Model weights fetched from mutable HF refs with no checksum or signature
findings.description: All GGUF/ONNX model weights are downloaded from `https://huggingface.co/<repo>/resolve/main/<file>` — `main` is a mutable branch pointer, not a pinned revision — and nothing verifies the bytes. The container entrypoints only test the first four bytes for the ASCII magic 'GGUF' (aligner-service/entrypoint.sh:25, diar-service/entrypoint.sh:25), which any attacker-supplied or truncated GGUF trivially satisfies. polyschnack-manage.sh:151 fetches the same URLs with `wget -qO ... || true`, so a failed or partial download is swallowed entirely. Affected repos include cstr/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3-GGUF, cstr/ark-asr-3b-GGUF, cstr/canary-1b-v2-GGUF, cstr/moonshine-base-de-fidoriel-GGUF and OpenVoiceOS/qwen3-asr-0.6b-q8-0 — all third-party community re-quantizations, not vendor-published artifacts. A GGUF is parsed by a C++ tensor loader; a malicious one is a memory-safety attack surface, and a silently swapped model is an undetectable output-integrity problem.
findings.evidence: parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3-q8_0.gguf: https://huggingface.co/cstr/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3-GGUF/resolve/main/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3-q8_0.gguf
findings.recommendation: Pin each model to an immutable commit SHA (`/resolve/<commit-sha>/`) and record an expected sha256 next to each entry in backends.yaml; have the entrypoints and manage.sh verify the digest before use and refuse to start on mismatch. Drop the `|| true` so download failures are loud.

findings.title: `selfupdate` overwrites the management script from the network without signature verification
findings.description: `polyschnack-manage.sh selfupdate` curls the script from raw.githubusercontent.com (or a GitLab API base) and replaces itself in place. The only validation is `bash -n` (syntax parses) and `wc -c > 1000` — neither says anything about authenticity. backends.yaml is replaced by the same mechanism (line 383) with only a grep for `^services:` and `model_files:`. The operator runs this script as the Docker-privileged user on the host, so a compromised mirror, a hijacked GitHub account, or any MITM on that fetch yields host-level code execution on the next invocation.
findings.evidence: if bash -n "$TMP" && [ "$(wc -c < "$TMP")" -gt 1000 ]; then chmod +x "$TMP"; mv "$TMP" "$0"
findings.recommendation: Ship a detached signature (minisign/cosign/GPG) alongside the script and backends.yaml and verify it before `mv`; or drop selfupdate in favour of `git pull` on a checkout whose commits are signed.

findings.title: Model URLs from network-fetched YAML are interpolated into `sh -c` inside a container
findings.description: `_model_req` builds MODELS_SCRIPT by string concatenation of the filename and URL parsed out of backends.yaml, then line 227 executes the whole accumulated string via `docker run --rm -v "$PWD/DATA/models:/models" alpine sh -c "$MODELS_SCRIPT ..."`. The URL is only single-quoted, so a value containing `'` closes the quote and injects arbitrary shell into a container that has the host's DATA/models directory mounted read-write. Combined with the unverified `selfupdate` of backends.yaml above, an attacker who controls the catalog file controls that shell. The `alpine` image is also referenced with no tag at all, so it resolves to `alpine:latest`.
findings.evidence: MODELS_SCRIPT="$MODELS_SCRIPT [ -s /models/$file ] || wget -qO /models/$file '$url' || true;"
findings.recommendation: Pass filenames and URLs as positional arguments to a fixed inline script (`sh -c 'script' _ "$file" "$url"`) rather than interpolating, validate each URL against an allowlist of `https://huggingface.co/` prefixes, and pin the alpine image by digest.

findings.title: qwen3-asr.cpp compiled from unpinned upstream HEAD with recursive submodules
findings.description: Both the qwen3 ASR image and the aligner image (aligner-service/Dockerfile:27) do `git clone --recursive https://github.com/predict-woo/qwen3-asr.cpp.git .` with no `--branch`/commit pin, then cmake-build whatever landed on the default branch and its submodules (ggml family) at build time. This is a single-maintainer research repository. Every CI run can produce a materially different binary from the same commit of this repo, and any upstream push — or submodule pointer change — lands as native code inside a container that later parses untrusted audio uploads.
findings.evidence: RUN git clone --recursive https://github.com/predict-woo/qwen3-asr.cpp.git .
findings.recommendation: Pin to a reviewed commit (`git clone ... && git checkout <sha> && git submodule update --init --recursive`) exposed as a build ARG, and bump it deliberately. Consider vendoring or mirroring the repo.

findings.title: CrispASR release tarballs downloaded and executed without checksum verification
findings.description: Five images (ark-asr-cpp:21, diar-service:26, canary-asr-cpp:21, moonshine-de-cpp:21, pk-asr-cpp:30) `wget -q` two pre-compiled tarballs from github.com/CrispStrobe/CrispASR releases, untar them and install the binaries plus a shared library (libc2pa_c.so) into /usr/local. There is no sha256sum, no signature, and no `--https-only`; the version is a git *tag* (ARG CRISPASR_VERSION), and GitHub release assets attached to a tag can be replaced without the tag changing. Version drift also exists: ark-asr-cpp pins v0.8.24 while diar/canary/moonshine/pk all pin v0.8.25, so the same wrapper logic ships two different binaries across the stack.
findings.evidence: RUN wget -q "https://github.com/CrispStrobe/CrispASR/releases/download/${CRISPASR_VERSION}/crispasr-linux-x86_64-cuda.tar.gz" -O /tmp/crispasr-cuda.tar.gz && tar xzf ...
findings.recommendation: Record the expected sha256 of each tarball as a build ARG and `sha256sum -c` before extracting; align all five images on one CRISPASR_VERSION (ideally defined once and passed in from CI).

findings.title: Webapp image builds ignore every lockfile in the repository
findings.description: webapp/uv.lock exists (70 pinned packages) but the Dockerfile copies only `pyproject.toml` before running `uv sync` — with no lock present, uv resolves fresh against PyPI on every build, so the image contents are unrelated to the committed lock and to what CI tested. The frontend stage does `COPY frontend/package.json frontend/package-lock.json* ./` followed by `npm install`: the glob makes the lock optional and `npm install` is free to rewrite it, whereas `npm ci` would enforce it. Line 27 additionally installs `yt-dlp>=2026.05.29` with an open upper bound, outside pyproject.toml and outside the lock — yt-dlp ships a large body of per-site extractor code and is invoked as a subprocess on user-supplied URLs (webapp/app/routers/url_import.py:66).
findings.evidence: COPY pyproject.toml ./\nRUN uv pip install --system "yt-dlp>=2026.05.29"\nRUN uv sync
findings.recommendation: `COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock ./` and use `uv sync --frozen` (fail on drift); switch the frontend stage to `COPY frontend/package.json frontend/package-lock.json ./` + `npm ci`; move yt-dlp into pyproject.toml with an exact version so it is covered by the lock.

findings.title: approach-a service dependencies are entirely unpinned and installed as root with --break-system-packages
findings.description: The ASR service image installs from requirements.txt where 12 of 14 entries are open-ended `>=` with no upper bound: onnx-asr[hub]>=0.10.0, fastapi>=0.115.0, uvicorn[standard]>=0.30.0, python-multipart>=0.0.9, silero-vad>=6.0.0, waitress>=3.0.0, flask>=3.0.0, openai>=1.0.0, typing_extensions>=4.0.0, psutil>=5.0.0, requests>=2.0.0, noisereduce>=3.0.0. Only onnxruntime-gpu==1.28.0 and numpy<2 are constrained. `openai>=1.0.0` and `requests>=2.0.0` in particular will happily absorb future major versions. approach-a/uv.lock exists but locks a *different* project (polyschnack-bench: gtts, jiwer, miniaudio — 21 packages) and never covers the service, so the deployed image has no lockfile at all. Dockerfile:35 installs with `pip install --no-cache-dir --break-system-packages` as root; a `polyschnack` user is created at line 26 but Dockerfile:48 explicitly declines to use it, so the container runs as root.
findings.evidence: onnx-asr[hub]>=0.10.0 / openai>=1.0.0 / requests>=2.0.0 / RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --break-system-packages -r requirements.txt
findings.recommendation: Generate a hash-pinned constraints file (`uv pip compile --generate-hashes`) for the service and install with `--require-hashes` into a venv rather than the system Python; then actually `USER polyschnack` and fix the model-volume ownership instead of staying root.

findings.title: node:20-slim base image is past end-of-life
findings.description: The frontend build stage uses `node:20-slim`. Node.js 20 'Iron' reached end-of-life on 2026-04-30 (confirmed against the Node.js release schedule) and no longer receives security patches, so the base layer accumulates unpatched OpenSSL/V8/npm issues. The same version is used in CI (.gitlab-ci.yml:49 `image: node:20-slim`, .github/workflows/ci.yml:45 `node-version: 20`). This is a build-time toolchain rather than a runtime image, which limits exposure, but the npm client and its TLS stack in that image are what fetch 318 packages from the registry.
findings.evidence: FROM node:20-slim AS fe
findings.recommendation: Move to node:22-slim (supported until 2027-04-30) or node:24-slim across the Dockerfile and both CI configs, pinned by digest.

findings.title: Base images pinned by tag only, with `latest` in several places
findings.description: No image anywhere in the repo is pinned by digest. `nvidia/cuda:12.8.0-devel-ubuntu24.04` and `-runtime-ubuntu24.04` (all nine Dockerfiles), `ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:python3.12-bookworm-slim` (webapp/Dockerfile:20), `python:3.12-slim`/`3.11-slim`/`3.13-slim` and `${HARBOR_REGISTRY}/public/ci-tools` (.gitlab-ci.yml) are all mutable tags. Explicit `latest` appears at compose.yml:17 (`tecnativa/docker-socket-proxy:latest`, a container that proxies the host Docker socket), .gitlab-ci.yml:242 (`alpine:latest` for the mirror job that handles the GitHub PAT), polyschnack-manage.sh:227 (bare `alpine`), and every service entry in compose.yml / compose.gpu.yml / compose.backends.yml / compose.benchmark.yml (`…/polyschnack-asr*:latest`). ci_smart_build.sh pushes both `:latest` and `:${CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA}`, but only `:latest` is what deployments consume, so a rollback or a pinned deploy is impossible.
findings.evidence: image: tecnativa/docker-socket-proxy:latest   /   image: ${REGISTRY:-ghcr.io/tilllt}/polyschnack-asr-webapp:latest
findings.recommendation: Pin third-party bases by `name:tag@sha256:…` (Renovate/Dependabot can bump them), and have compose consume `${POLYSCHNACK_TAG:-latest}` so a deployment can be nailed to a commit SHA tag.

findings.title: Webapp lockfile drags in torch plus the full NVIDIA CUDA wheel stack
findings.description: The Dockerfile comment at webapp/Dockerfile:29-31 claims 'Kein CUDA-torch mehr in der Webapp … Die Webapp bleibt CPU-only (~2,5-3 GB kleiner)', but the resolved lock contains torch@2.13.0, torchaudio@2.11.0, triton@3.7.1 and eighteen nvidia-*/cuda-* wheels (nvidia-cublas@13.1.1.3, nvidia-cudnn-cu13@9.20.0.48, nvidia-nccl-cu13@2.29.7, cuda-toolkit@13.0.3.0, …). They arrive transitively through `silero-vad>=6.0.0`, which is used only for voice-activity detection. That is multiple gigabytes of native CUDA code and a very large attack/CVE surface added to a container that is meant to be a CPU-only FastAPI frontend. Total transitive count: 70 packages for 11 direct dependencies.
findings.evidence: torch@2.13.0, triton@3.7.1, nvidia-cublas@13.1.1.3, nvidia-cudnn-cu13@9.20.0.48, nvidia-nccl-cu13@2.29.7 … (webapp/uv.lock)
findings.recommendation: Install the CPU torch wheel explicitly via a uv index override (`torch` from the pytorch cpu index), or replace silero-vad with an ONNX-runtime-based VAD; then re-check the resolved lock actually matches the CPU-only claim in the comment.

findings.title: GitHub Actions referenced by mutable tag rather than commit SHA
findings.description: `actions/checkout@v4`, `actions/setup-python@v5` and `actions/setup-node@v4` are referenced by floating major tags. These are GitHub-maintained actions, so the practical risk is lower than for third-party actions, but a moved tag still means the workflow silently runs different code — and this workflow runs on `pull_request`, i.e. it is reachable by outside contributors on the public mirror.
findings.evidence: - uses: actions/checkout@v4
findings.recommendation: Pin each action to a full commit SHA with the version in a trailing comment, and let Dependabot bump them.

findings.title: CI installs test dependencies unpinned and hides installation failures
findings.description: Test jobs pip-install ad-hoc floating dependency sets rather than the committed locks — `pip install -q pytest httpx fastapi "sqlmodel>=0.0.16" "pydantic>=2" python-multipart numpy cryptography authlib itsdangerous pyyaml 2>/dev/null` — so the versions under test bear no relation to the versions in the images, and CI results are not reproducible across days. The trailing `2>/dev/null` (also on lines 12, 28, 52 and 218) discards installer errors; the frontend job papers over this further with `npm install … 2>/dev/null || npm install …`. The Python version also differs from production: test-core runs python:3.11-slim while approach-a's image builds on Python 3.12, and test-webapp runs 3.13 against a 3.12 image.
findings.evidence: pip install -q pytest httpx fastapi "sqlmodel>=0.0.16" ... 2>/dev/null
findings.recommendation: Install via `uv sync --frozen --group dev` / `npm ci` from the committed locks, drop the `2>/dev/null` redirections, and match the interpreter versions used in the images.

findings.title: esbuild 0.21.5 in the frontend tree is affected by the dev-server CORS advisory
findings.description: The lock resolves esbuild@0.21.5 (transitively via vite@5.4.21). esbuild versions <= 0.24.2 set `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on the development server, letting any visited website read source from a developer's running dev server (GHSA-67mh-4wv8-2f99). This only affects `npm run dev` on a developer machine, never the built image, since the Docker build only runs `vite build`. The tree also carries two major versions of vite simultaneously — vite@5.4.21 for the build and vite@8.2.0 pulled in by vitest@4.1.10 — which is duplicated toolchain surface and a sign the two are due for alignment.
findings.evidence: node_modules/esbuild @ 0.21.5 (hasInstallScript), vite@5.4.21 + vite@8.2.0
findings.recommendation: Upgrade vite to a line that carries esbuild >= 0.25 so the dev server is not world-readable, and align the vite version used by vitest with the build's.

findings.title: Aligner entrypoint sends a literal `Bearer ***` instead of the HF token
findings.description: The aligner's download uses `${HF_TOKEN:+-H "Authorization: Bearer ***"}` — the redaction placeholder was left in the code path rather than in a log line, so when HF_TOKEN is set the request carries a literal three-asterisk credential. The equivalent line in diar-service/entrypoint.sh:43 correctly interpolates `${HF_TOKEN}`. Any gated-repo model download from the aligner therefore fails with a 401 and falls into the manual-download error path, and the discrepancy makes it easy to believe the token is being honoured when it is not.
findings.evidence: ${HF_TOKEN:+-H "Authorization: Bearer ***"} \
findings.recommendation: Use `${HF_TOKEN:+-H "Authorization: Bearer ${HF_TOKEN}"}` as diar-service does, and keep redaction confined to echo/log statements.

findings.title: No image signing, SBOM, or provenance for the nine published images
findings.description: The build script does a plain `docker build` + `docker push` of `:latest` and `:${SHA}`, and the mirror-ghcr job re-pushes those tags to the public ghcr.io/tilllt namespace. Nothing produces an SBOM, signs the images, or attaches provenance, so a downstream consumer pulling `ghcr.io/tilllt/polyschnack-asr-webapp:latest` (which is what compose.yml defaults to) has no way to verify origin. The SHA guard also means that if a `:${SHA}` tag already exists the build is skipped and `:latest` is simply re-tagged from it — correct for idempotency, but it also means a tag pushed by anything other than this pipeline would be silently trusted and promoted to `:latest`. Registry credentials themselves are handled acceptably: `${CONFIG_JSON}` is a masked CI file variable and GHCR_TOKEN is piped via `--password-stdin`; no secrets appear in build ARGs or in any Dockerfile.
findings.evidence: docker build -t "${SRC}:latest" -t "${SRC}:${SHA}" "$CTX" ; docker push "${SRC}:latest"
findings.recommendation: Add `docker buildx build --sbom=true --provenance=mode=max` and cosign keyless signing in the build job, and verify signatures in the mirror job before promoting to ghcr.io.

findings.title: Dependency hygiene that is in good shape
findings.description: Noting the positives so they are not accidentally regressed: package-lock.json is lockfileVersion 3 with 318 packages, every one carrying an `integrity` hash and resolving from registry.npmjs.org — no git or tarball URLs, no scoped-name typosquat lookalikes. Only esbuild and fsevents declare install scripts, both expected native-binary packages. No package.json lifecycle scripts run anything beyond tsc/vite/vitest. No `--trusted-host`, no `verify=False`, no `ssl._create_unverified_context`, no `--no-check-certificate`, and no `curl | sh` pattern appears anywhere in the Dockerfiles, CI configs or scripts. The only plaintext http:// URL is the internal `http://docker-proxy:2375` service address on the compose network. Direct dependency choices are mainstream and maintained (fastapi 0.141.0, cryptography 49.0.0, sqlmodel 0.0.39, react 18.3.1, @tanstack/react-query 5.101.4) with no abandoned or disreputable packages spotted.
findings.evidence: 318 packages, 0 missing integrity, 0 non-registry resolved URLs
findings.recommendation: Keep it that way — enable `npm audit` (currently disabled via --no-audit in both CI configs) and a `uv pip audit`/pip-audit step so regressions surface.

uniformity.summary: Within each layer the codebase is more consistent than its size suggests: HTTP is 100% httpx (zero requests/aiohttp), there are zero bare `except:`, logging in webapp/app is uniformly `log = logging.getLogger(__name__)` with %-style args and no f-strings, the frontend is 98% routed through src/api.ts with strict TypeScript and only 2 `any`, and 20 of 20 components follow PascalCase + named-export + interface-Props. The real divergence is between what CONTRIBUTING.md declares and what the code does: it mandates `uv run ruff check` and `uv run mypy` (neither tool is a dependency, has a config file, or runs in CI), `async def` for I/O-bound handlers (69 of 75 endpoints are sync `def`, and all 3 non-auth `async` endpoints block the event loop on subprocess/sync-httpx/file I/O), DB logic in crud.py (54 inline session.exec/add/commit calls across 11 routers), and Pydantic v2 (0 uses of `response_model`; 75 endpoints return raw dicts with 35 `Dict[str, Any]` vs 26 `dict` annotations). Two large dead-code twins survive because nothing lints for them: webapp/app/asr_client.py (203 lines) is shadowed by the asr_client/ package, and approach-a/app.py (1104 lines, 49 print() calls) is unreachable since the Dockerfile runs server.py. Language is the most visible split — ~86% of frontend comments and most Python comments are German while docs/API.md and grouping.ts/format.ts are pure English, and /benchmark ships ~20 hardcoded German strings to en/pt-BR users. Infrastructure conventions drift the same way: 5 CrispASR Dockerfiles duplicate a 25-line block verbatim, only 1 of 8 Dockerfiles has a HEALTHCHECK, 1 of 4 compose services lacks one, only 3 of 9 shell scripts use `set -euo pipefail`, and CI tests on Python 3.11/3.13 while the runtime image is 3.12.

findings.title: CONTRIBUTING.md mandates ruff + mypy, but neither is installed, configured, or run anywhere
findings.description: The declared pre-MR gate is `uv run ruff check .` and `uv run mypy .`. Neither tool appears in webapp/pyproject.toml or approach-a/pyproject.toml dependencies or dev-dependencies, there is no ruff.toml / [tool.ruff] / [tool.mypy] / setup.cfg / .flake8 / .pre-commit-config.yaml / .editorconfig anywhere in the repo, and neither .gitlab-ci.yml nor .github/workflows/ci.yml invokes them. This is the root cause of every other drift in this report: nothing mechanically enforces any convention, so 25.8k lines of Python have diverged by hand.
findings.evidence: grep -rn 'ruff|mypy' webapp/pyproject.toml approach-a/pyproject.toml .gitlab-ci.yml .github/workflows/ci.yml -> 0 hits. find for ruff.toml/.flake8/.pre-commit-config.yaml/.editorconfig -> 0 hits.
findings.recommendation: Add ruff + mypy to webapp dev deps with a shared [tool.ruff] config at repo root, wire a `lint` job into .gitlab-ci.yml and .github/workflows/ci.yml, and start with `ruff check --select F` (undefined/unused names) which alone would flag the two dead modules below.

findings.title: All three non-auth async endpoints block the event loop; the convention says the opposite of what the code does
findings.description: CONTRIBUTING.md line 96 states: 'Async: `async def` fuer I/O-gebundene Route-Handler; sync fuer reine CPU-Arbeit'. In practice 69 of 75 endpoints are sync `def` (which FastAPI correctly runs in a threadpool), and the 6 `async def` handlers are the problem: `import_from_url` calls blocking `subprocess.run(['yt-dlp', ...], timeout=600)` twice (url_import.py:64 and :86) directly on the event loop, so one YouTube import can stall the entire server for up to 20 minutes; `upload_recording` (recordings.py:486) does blocking `stored.write_bytes()` at :541 and an ffprobe subprocess via `probe_duration_path()` at :549; `create_transcription` (openai_proxy.py:84) awaits nothing after `file.read()` and then calls the adapters, which are all sync `httpx.Client` (12 sites, e.g. asr_client/adapters/pk_cpp.py:50 with `timeout=3600`). Only the 3 authlib handlers in auth.py genuinely need async. So the async/sync split is inverted relative to the stated rule AND the six exceptions are the six most blocking operations in the app.
findings.evidence: async endpoints=6 (auth.py:98,119,164; recordings.py:486; openai_proxy.py:84; url_import.py:37) vs sync def endpoints=69. httpx.Client (sync) = 12 sites in webapp/app, httpx.AsyncClient = 0 in webapp/app (only approach-a/benchmark.py, a CLI). url_import.py:64 `subprocess.run(..., timeout=600)` inside `async def`.
findings.recommendation: Either drop `async` from upload_recording / import_from_url / create_transcription so FastAPI threadpools them (one-word fix, matches the other 69 endpoints), or wrap the blocking calls in `starlette.concurrency.run_in_threadpool`. Then reword the CONTRIBUTING rule to describe the actual, defensible convention: sync `def` everywhere except OAuth flows.

findings.title: webapp/app/asr_client.py (203 lines) is dead code shadowed by the asr_client/ package
findings.description: Both `webapp/app/asr_client.py` and `webapp/app/asr_client/__init__.py` exist. Python resolves the package, so the 203-line module is unreachable: every importer (`from ..asr_client import get_client` in openai_proxy.py:25 and models.py:14, `from .asr_client import get_client` in service.py:20, and 6 test files) gets the package. The two files even share the same opening docstring ('HTTP client for the ASR inference service'), so a reader grepping for `transcribe()` finds two near-identical implementations with different timeouts and no indication which one runs. asr_client.py also holds a third `time.sleep(1)` retry loop (line 187) duplicating adapters/pk_python.py:151.
findings.evidence: ls webapp/app/asr_client.py webapp/app/asr_client/__init__.py -> both present (7012 and 12025 bytes). Both start with the identical docstring line. No importer can reach the .py module.
findings.recommendation: Delete webapp/app/asr_client.py. Verify first with `python -c 'import app.asr_client as m; print(m.__file__)'` from webapp/ — it will print the package __init__.py.

findings.title: approach-a/app.py (1104 lines, 49 print calls) is a dead second server implementation still COPYed into the image
findings.description: approach-a contains two complete server implementations. The live one is `server.py` (38 lines) -> `polyschnack_service/` (FastAPI, `logger.warning/exception` with %-style args, HTTPException error handling, 5 modules). The dead one is `app.py`: 1104 lines with its own ONNX loading, silence-based chunking, waitress thread config, `sys.stdout = sys.stderr` at line 18, wildcard `import os, sys, json, math, re, threading` at line 20, and 49 `print()` calls used as logging (`print('\u26a0\ufe0f Invalid ... value')` at line 54). The Dockerfile CMD is `python server.py` (line 73) yet still does `COPY app.py .` (line 40) and `COPY templates/ templates/` (line 41). No Python file imports it. This single file accounts for 49 of the 149 print() calls in the repo and is the main reason the repo looks like it mixes print and logging.
findings.evidence: approach-a/Dockerfile:73 `CMD ["python", "server.py"]`; approach-a/Dockerfile:40 `COPY app.py .`. grep for `import app`/`from app import` in approach-a -> only a comment in test_model_selection.py:16. print() per file: app.py 49, benchmark.py 23, polyschnack_service/* 0.
findings.recommendation: Delete approach-a/app.py and templates/, and drop lines 40-41 from approach-a/Dockerfile. After that the only remaining print() calls in shipped service code are aligner_server.py:446/452 (startup messages, acceptable) and service_registry.py:106 (under a __main__ self-check).

findings.title: Zero response_model across 75 endpoints; return annotations split 4 ways and half the endpoints are undocumented
findings.description: CONTRIBUTING.md line 93 declares 'FastAPI + Pydantic v2', and 11 routers do define 30 BaseModel classes — but exclusively for *request* bodies. `response_model` appears 0 times in webapp/app. Responses are hand-built dicts, annotated inconsistently: 35 `-> Dict[str, Any]`, 26 `-> dict`, 4 `-> List[Dict[str, Any]]`, 6 bare `-> list`, 1 `-> List[dict]`, 1 `-> Any`. Serialization helpers exist in only 3 of 11 CRUD routers (`_recording_to_dict` recordings.py:399, `_key_response` keys.py:47, `_to_dict` llm_endpoints.py:48); templates.py:65, targets.py:74, shares.py:69 and versions.py:67 inline the dict literal in the return statement. 38 of 75 endpoints have no docstring. Net effect: the generated /docs and the hand-written api_specs.py (493 lines of literal OpenAPI JSON) cannot be reconciled, and api_specs.py must be updated by hand whenever a route changes.
findings.evidence: grep -c response_model webapp/app -> 0. Return annotation tally across routers: Dict[str,Any]=35, dict=26, list=6, List[Dict[str,Any]]=4. BaseModel classes=30 across 11 routers, all request-side. Endpoints with docstring: 37/75.
findings.recommendation: Pick one: either add `response_model=` with Pydantic response models (and let FastAPI generate the spec, shrinking api_specs.py to the non-FastAPI backends only), or accept raw dicts and normalise every annotation to `dict[str, Any]` / `list[dict[str, Any]]`. Do not leave the current 4-way split.

findings.title: DB logic inline in 11 of 19 routers despite the 'never in route handlers' rule
findings.description: CONTRIBUTING.md line 95: 'DB-Logik | Liegt in `crud.py` - nie inline in Route-Handlern'. crud.py has 16 functions and is imported by 7 routers, but there are 54 direct `session.exec(...)` / `session.add(...)` / `session.commit()` calls spread across 11 routers: recordings.py 11, shares.py 10, keys.py 6, llm_endpoints.py 6, targets.py 6, templates.py 6, segments.py 4, versions.py 2, auth.py 1, url_import.py 1, recovery.py 1. Some routers (shares, keys, targets, templates) do all their persistence inline and never touch crud.py at all, so there is no single place to add e.g. a tenant filter or soft-delete.
findings.evidence: 54 inline session.exec/add/commit calls across 11 router files; crud.py exports 16 functions; 7 routers import it.
findings.recommendation: Either move the per-entity queries into crud.py (or per-entity crud modules, given 16 functions is already crowded), or delete the rule from CONTRIBUTING.md and document the actual pattern. The current half-state means new code has no clear precedent to copy.

findings.title: No logging configuration in the webapp: all 32 log.info calls are silently discarded in production
findings.description: 24 modules do `log = logging.getLogger(__name__)` and emit 34 log.warning / 32 log.info / 15 log.exception / 1 log.error / 1 log.debug calls — the style itself is admirably uniform (0 f-strings in log calls, 44 %-style placeholders). But there is no `logging.basicConfig` or `dictConfig` anywhere in webapp/app, and uvicorn only configures the `uvicorn*` loggers, not the root logger. App loggers therefore fall through to `logging.lastResort`, which is fixed at WARNING — every `log.info` in the webapp is dropped, including the ones that exist specifically to trace job progress. The only basicConfig in the repo is approach-a/polyschnack_service/config.py:186, which is a different service.
findings.evidence: grep -rn 'basicConfig|dictConfig|setLevel' *.py -> 1 hit, approach-a/polyschnack_service/config.py:186. webapp/app has 0. Level tally in webapp/app: warning 34, info 32, exception 15, error 1, debug 1.
findings.recommendation: Add a `logging.basicConfig(level=os.getenv('LOG_LEVEL','INFO'), format=...)` in main.py before app creation (or a uvicorn log_config), matching what approach-a/polyschnack_service/config.py:186 already does — that would also make the two services log identically.

findings.title: Frontend has four competing ways to surface an error, including window.alert and 9 silent swallows
